beats.narration_text: Ciao. This is Liam, in for Bear. In C S Y E seven two seven zero, an A. I. writes the code for your games. The shortcut is to think that leaves nothing for you to do. This film is about the opposite: what is left, and why it is the whole job.

beats.narration_text: Five terms. Conducting means directing an A. I.'s work: choosing the goal, hearing what is off, and deciding what goes out. A coding agent is an A. I. that reads your project, edits it, and runs commands. To verify is to check an answer against the real thing, not against the A. I.'s say-so. A receipt is a saved record of what a check found. And play-feel is whether a game feels right in the hands, which only a person can judge.

terms.meaning: directing an AI's work: the goal, the doubt, the decision
an AI that reads your project, edits it, and runs commands
check against the real thing, not the AI's say-so
a saved record of what a check found
whether a game feels right in the hands

beats.narration_text: In this course, the A. I. writes the code. Claude Code or Codex reads your project, edits it, runs it, and reports back. You do not type the game.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'The Empty Podium' (serif 40) top-left. A grey-outlined page: seven grey lines write themselves in one by one with a terracotta cursor dot (the AI writes the code). The page becomes the tool's window, headed 'Claude Code', tagged 'recorded run', and the four REAL tool calls of the recorded Godot run land as rows (Read pong.tscn, Edit pong.tscn, Write check_label.gd, godot --headless …) then a check and PASS. After the midpoint the REAL Walker Jumpman capture (Clawd running and jumping, Godot 4.7.2, scripted input) fades in on the right in a grey frame, labelled 'Walker Jumpman', and plays frame by frame. Last: a keyboard drawn in grey with an ink prohibition ring over it.

beats.narration_text: Picture an orchestra where every player has just got better. Every instrument improved, and nobody is conducting. Each player is brilliant. Nobody is holding the whole performance. The podium is empty.

Seats drop in ('orchestra'); a terracotta light comes on at every seat ('every player has just got better'); every instrument grows taller ('every instrument improved'); a dashed grey baton outline draws over the podium ('nobody is conducting'); a spark visits every seat in turn ('each player is brilliant'); a dashed ring draws around all the players ('the whole performance', labelled); lights dim, the baton outline turns ink and 'empty podium' appears ('the podium is empty').
shot.motion_claim: Every seat lights up and every instrument grows, while the podium stays empty and the baton outline is only dashed.

beats.narration_text: That is a game built by an A. I. with nobody directing. Each script can be fluent. Each scene can look right. And the game can still be wrong, because nobody held the whole thing.

beats.act: II · What the AI Does, What You Do
beats.narration_text: Start with an asymmetry. Making an answer and checking an answer are different jobs. The A. I. made the first one cheap. It did not make the second one cheap.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'What the AI Does, What You Do' (serif 40) top-left. A grey maker block at the left of a one-lane channel, a wall with ONE person-sized slot and an unlit lamp at the right, a pass tray beyond it. On 'making an answer' a kraft crate (a game part) leaves the maker (label 'make') and rolls to the wall; on 'checking an answer' the lamp lights (terracotta dot, label 'check') and the crate passes the slot slowly to the tray where an ink check lands. On 'made the first one cheap' five crates stream out of the maker at once and queue at the wall ('cheap' with a check). On 'did not make the second one cheap' only one crate inches through the slot ('not cheap' with a cross).

show.event: lamp lit: 'check'; crate passes slowly to the tray, check mark
one crate through the slot: 'not cheap' + cross

shot.motion_claim: Crates pour out of the maker fast while the same wall passes one crate at a time: making is cheap, checking is not.

lecture.runner_up: Isometric kraft-box conveyor with a gate (show-tell iso_kit), auditioned in low-res: the oblique crate on a flat channel reads the same and keeps the slot visibly one crate wide, and the same cast carries B07-B08.
lecture.why: A channel and a wall with a slot IS the claim (rate of making vs rate of checking); the voice can point at crates pouring out against one crate passing.

beats.act: II · What the AI Does, What You Do
beats.narration_text: And it gets harder, not easier. The faster the A. I. makes things, the more there is to check. The channel for making gets wider. The gate for checking stays person-sized.

shot.visual_intent: Same cast as B06: three crates already queued at the one-slot wall. On 'The faster the A.I. makes things' the maker pushes four more crates and the queue backs up to the maker. On 'The channel for making gets wider' the channel's roof lifts (a double-headed dimension arrow, label 'wider') and two more rows of crates fill it, all piling against the same wall. On 'the gate stays person-sized' a dimension arrow measures the slot, the Professor Bear portrait ('you') appears beside it with the label 'person-sized'.

shot.motion_claim: The channel widens and the pile-up grows; the slot does not change, and a person's height measures it.

lecture.runner_up: Remotion DesignPipelineClaim with diagramStyle show-tell-isometric (blocked outputs stop at a barrier); it cannot widen one side while the gate holds, and its labels are fixed per stage.

beats.act: II · What the AI Does, What You Do
beats.narration_text: Be careful with that claim. It is an argument with limits, not a law. A tool that runs your game and measures it does check something. But a person chose that check. And a person decides whether the result is what was meant.

shot.visual_intent: Top-left: a person-sized gate drawn in dashed grey with the label 'argument, not law'. On 'A tool that runs your game and measures it' a grey pane 'recorded receipt' fills line by line with the REAL lines of mechanics-1789103433.44707.json ("id": "fixed-jump-and-no-double", "rise_px": 56.07470703125, "status": "PASS", ellipses between) and an ink check lands on PASS. On 'a person chose that check' the Professor Bear portrait appears with a grey arrow and a terracotta dot to the "id" line; on 'decides whether the result is what was meant' the arrow moves to the rise_px line and a leader reaches the label 'meant?'.

show.event: portrait + arrow to the id line

shot.motion_claim: The tool's real output arrives and is ticked; then a person's arrow lands first on which check, then on whether the number is what was meant.

lecture.runner_up: Remotion CCPlainShell with the same lines: it spaces ~13 lines evenly and cannot point at one line, and the pointing is the claim.
lecture.why: A real receipt shown as itself, with a person's pointer, shows both limits of the claim (a tool does check; a person chose it and judges it).

beats.act: II · What the AI Does, What You Do
beats.narration_text: You do the deciding. You decide what the game is for, and who it is for. An A. I. will build any version you hand it, flawlessly, including the wrong one.

shot.visual_intent: The Professor Bear portrait ('you') at the left of a grey page headed 'GAME-BRIEF.md' holding two real lines of the project's own brief: the concept (Clawd, a coding agent, goes through an agentic loop on every level) and who it is for (keyboard players who know what a coding agent is). On 'any version you hand it' three real options for one open design question land as rows ((a) undo most recent task, station re-reachable; (b) undo becomes a 2 s freeze; (c) malware is a plain hazard, no undo); on 'flawlessly' an ink check lands on each; on 'the wrong one' the label 'which is wrong?' appears and a terracotta dot walks the three rows and stops on none.
shot.motion_claim: All three versions get an equal check: the machine builds each one flawlessly, and only the person's question 'which is wrong?' is left.

qc.sparse_reason: brief page plus three rows on cream; fills as the rows land

lecture.runner_up: Three real game stills (Walker Jumpman, Pong, Dodge the Creeps) as 'three versions': they are three different games, not versions of one brief, so the picture would misstate the claim.
lecture.why: The project's own open question with its real options says 'any version, flawlessly' with a real artifact instead of a stock picture.

beats.act: II · What the AI Does, What You Do
beats.narration_text: You hear that something is wrong before any check says so. A jump that cannot clear the gap. An enemy that cannot be dodged. A number that is too perfect.

Then three outline panels labelled 'drawn examples': (1) Clawd's arc ends in the gap before the far ledge ('gap too wide'); (2) a column of spikes fills the corridor from floor to roof with Clawd stuck at its left ('no way past'); (3) a big '100%' ('too perfect'). The player is a drawn grey stand-in; everything in the panels is drawn.

Card 2: one jump arc with a second arc stacked on its apex, 'two jump arcs'. Card 3: eighteen small squares (6 x 3), 'mistaken for abilities'.
shot.motion_claim: Each card is filled in the moment its prediction is spoken: the body drawn against the box, the second arc growing on the first, eighteen squares counted out.
